passage: Avni, I've watched you say "no problem" to everyone this month, and it reminds me of someone. Thirty years ago at this press, we had a proofreader called Mohan. Whoever was late, Mohan stayed back. Whoever fought, Mohan made tea and calmed them down. We all liked him, and none of us noticed that he hadn't had a raise in four years. When a new manager, Mrs Kurian, arrived, she read the night logs and saw his name on every late shift. At the next meeting she thanked him by name and split the late shifts on a rota. Mohan went red and said it was nothing. It wasn't. Things ran better once the load was shared. So, Avni, who is going to see your name in the logs?

qa.q: How long had Mohan gone without a raise?
qa.a: Mohan hadn't had a raise in four years.

qa.q: What does Mohan going red and calling it nothing suggest?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed by praise and unused to being noticed, though it clearly mattered.

qa.q: What choices did Mrs Kurian make after reading the night logs?
qa.a: She thanked Mohan by name and split the late shifts on a rota, sharing both the load and the credit.

qa.q: How might Mohan have felt about all those years of late shifts before Mrs Kurian noticed?
qa.a: He may have felt taken for granted, carrying the extra work quietly while nobody saw it.

grounding: A senior colleague remembers a helpful proofreader whose goodwill held the team together until a fair manager shared his load and recognition.

passage: The client demo was at four, the office generator had failed, and two of the team were stuck in a flooded underpass. Keerthana, leading the team for the first time, watched Alka do what she always did: find the spare laptop, calm the intern, rewrite the missing slides and fetch everyone water, without a word about herself. The demo went well. The client thanked Keerthana. Keerthana opened her mouth to say thank you, then noticed Alka already packing up to finish someone else's report. She checked the tracker: Alka's name was on nine tasks, most not her own. On the evening call she said, "The demo happened because of Alka," and moved four of those tasks to others. Alka blinked, surprised, then smiled.

qa.q: How many tasks was Alka's name on in the tracker?
qa.a: Alka's name was on nine tasks, most not her own.

qa.q: What does Alka's surprised blink on the evening call suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she is not used to being credited, and the recognition caught her off guard.

qa.q: What choices did Keerthana make after checking the tracker?
qa.a: She gave Alka credit on the call and moved four of her tasks to others, sharing both recognition and load.

qa.q: What might have happened to Alka if Keerthana had simply accepted the client's thanks?
qa.a: Alka's work would have stayed invisible and her load would have kept growing, risking burnout.

grounding: On a chaotic demo day a new team lead notices a supportive colleague is overloaded and unthanked, and shares the load and the credit.

passage: In her second week as team lead at the Bengaluru office, Sangeeta started a list: who does what. Asif's column kept growing. He had onboarded both new hires, remembered everyone's birthdays, taken the angry client calls nobody wanted, and stayed late fixing other people's bugs without a word. In meetings he said, 'Happy to help.' Then she opened the quarterly deck her predecessor had made. Seven names on the launch credits. Not Asif's. Sangeeta felt a flush of anger on his behalf, and a small guilt too: she had already asked him for two favours herself. On Friday she added his name to the credits, moved onboarding to a rota, and said in the team meeting, 'The launch held together because of Asif.' Asif looked down, embarrassed, then smiled properly for the first time she had seen.

qa.q: How many names were on the launch credits?
qa.a: Seven, and Asif's was not one of them.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta feel on seeing the credits?
qa.a: She felt a flush of anger on Asif's behalf, and a small guilt for having asked him for favours herself.

qa.q: Which of Sangeeta's steps shares the load, and which shares the recognition?
qa.a: The onboarding rota shares the load; adding his name to the credits and thanking him in the meeting shares the recognition.

qa.q: How might Asif feel when Sangeeta thanks him in the meeting?
qa.a: Asif is embarrassed but pleased, smiling properly, finally seen for work he never asked credit for.

grounding: Shows a new team lead noticing that an agreeable colleague holds the team together unthanked and overloaded, and sharing both the load and the recognition.

passage:
'Karthik, you're doing Manoj's slides again?'
'He's got a lot on. It's fine.'
'You've got a lot on. You did Leena's report on Monday. I've dumped things on you too, and I feel bad about it.'
'Everyone's stressed. Someone has to be the glue.'
'And when did you last ask for anything? The appraisal form had a box for achievements. You wrote two lines.'
Karthik laughed. 'I don't like making a fuss.'
'I'm going to say something to Meenakshi.'
'Please don't make it awkward.'
'I won't. I'll just tell her what I see.'
In the manager's cabin, Kiran said it plainly: 'Karthik holds this team together, and he's drowning. Half the slides you praised last month were his.' Meenakshi was quiet. 'I didn't know. Thank you.' That afternoon she handed Manoj's deck back to Manoj and asked Karthik to present his own work.

qa.q: How much did Karthik write in the appraisal box?
qa.a: Two lines.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while talking to Karthik?
qa.a: Kiran felt uneasy and a bit guilty for having dumped work on Karthik too, and worried that he was drowning.

qa.q: Was Kiran right to go to Meenakshi? Why?
qa.a: Yes; the manager could fix both the load and the credit, and Kiran spoke plainly without making it awkward for Karthik.

qa.q: What was the week like for Karthik before Meenakshi stepped in?
qa.a: Karthik was overloaded with other people's slides and reports, laughing it off because he dislikes fuss, while getting no credit.

grounding: Shows a colleague who notices an agreeable teammate being overloaded and unrecognised, and a manager who then shares the load and the credit.

passage: When I became project lead last year, I thought our team just got along naturally. I'm Raghav. It took me four months to see that it wasn't natural; it was Eshaan. He was the one who smoothed things over when two designers fought, who brought extra lunch when someone forgot theirs, who said yes every time I asked, 'Can anyone pick this up?' Then in March he was ill for a fortnight, and the team fell apart: arguments in every stand-up, deadlines slipping. I felt stupid, honestly. I'd built my calm team on one person's goodwill and never once thanked him in front of anyone. When he came back, I stopped asking 'can anyone' and started assigning. I nominated him for the quarterly award and wrote down exactly what he did. He read it and said, 'I didn't think anyone noticed.'

qa.q: What happened while Eshaan was ill in March?
qa.a: The team fell apart: arguments in every stand-up and deadlines slipping.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when the team fell apart?
qa.a: Raghav felt stupid and guilty for building a calm team on Eshaan's goodwill without ever thanking him.

qa.q: What changes did Raghav make, and why are they fair?
qa.a: Assigning work instead of asking 'can anyone', and nominating Eshaan with specifics, so both the load and the recognition are shared.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's 'I didn't think anyone noticed' reveal?
qa.a: Eshaan had felt his work was invisible, and was touched and surprised to be seen.

grounding: Shows a lead realising that an agreeable colleague's goodwill held the team together while he was overloaded and unthanked, and sharing the load and recognition.

passage:
Team lead's notes, Friday.
This week I watched how the team really runs. When the client moved the deadline, Usha stayed late to rebuild the slides for Chandrika, who was off sick. On Wednesday Usha quietly fixed two broken formulas in my own sheet and never mentioned it.
In the review meeting the slides were praised, and Usha's name came up nowhere. She smiled and kept taking notes.
When I asked her about the new onboarding project, she said, "Sure, happy to." Then I looked at the board: she already had four open tasks. I felt uncomfortable that I had nearly added a fifth.
What I did next: I moved two of her tasks to Imran and to myself. I named her work on the slides in the team email. I also put her forward for the review round in March, and asked her directly what she wants to grow into. She took a long time to answer.

qa.q: How many open tasks did Usha already have on the board?
qa.a: Usha already had four open tasks.

qa.q: What was the team lead feeling on seeing the board, and why?
qa.a: The team lead felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed at nearly adding a fifth task to Usha's four, after seeing how much of her work went unnoticed.

qa.q: Which of the team lead's steps shares the load fairly?
qa.a: Moving two of Usha's tasks to Imran and to the team lead spreads the work, and naming her in the team email and the review round shares the credit.

qa.q: What might it be like for Usha when her name is missing from the review meeting?
qa.a: Usha smiled and kept taking notes, but going unnamed again may leave her feeling invisible; her long pause when asked what she wants suggests she is not used to being asked.

grounding: Shows a team lead noticing an always-helpful colleague being overloaded and uncredited, and sharing out both the work and the recognition.
